newsitem.title: JAPAN: Charts show support for Japan stocks above 17,000.
newsitem.headline: Charts show support for Japan stocks above 17,000.

text.p: The pattern set by gyrating Japanese stocks over the last few sessions shows a technical support line above the 17,000 point level which is likely to hold for a while, analysts said on Tuesday.
The analysts said that in the wake of Monday's strong rebound by the Nikkei average, they could pinpoint a trough on technical charts that constitutes a support line for stocks.
Analysts said this was around 17,303 points, the Nikkei's closing low on Friday, or around 17,019, the intra-day low on Monday, which are 17-month lows.

They said stocks could retest these levels sometime in February, as the market still lacks confidence in Japan's economic recovery. A break through the floor could trigger an accelerated drop to new depths, they added.

The market's key index -- the Nikkei 225 average -- recovered more than 800 points on Monday after last week's accumulated loss of more than 2,000 points on worries about an economic downturn and scepticism about the government's commitment to reform.
On Tuesday, the Nikkei ended at 18,093.13, near Monday's close, after a volatile session that saw it plunging initially then popping briefly into positive territory.
"A sharp rebound after a nosedive forms a bottom on charts," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
"Although the market environment is still unclear, the Nikkei could remain on a recovery trend for now," he said.
"When the Nikkei nears 17,000 next time, buying demand will slow the fall," said a chartist at a major Japanese brokerage.
"But the Nikkei is still likely to head lower and form a triple bottom," he said.
Analysts said that if the Nikkei breached support at 17,000, there was no solid support line until close to 14,000.

This could set a third major bottom for the Nikkei since the start of Japan's economic recession in the early 1990s, following a 14,309 closing low for the Nikkei in 1992 and a 14,485 closing low in 1995.
Analysts said the market could come under selling pressure again in February, due to expected profit-taking before companies close their books at the end of March.
